practice_items.atom_title: Voice/image cloning for impersonation
practice_items.prompt: How much audio is typically needed to clone someone's voice with a modern synthesis model?
options: At least 30 minutes of clean recording
A full conversation of at least 5 minutes
3-10 seconds of audio
Audio cloning is not yet possible with consumer tools
practice_items.explain: Modern voice-cloning models can be fine-tuned on 3-10 seconds of audio, such as a voicemail greeting or short public video clip.

practice_items.atom_title: Voice/image cloning for impersonation
practice_items.prompt: Which of the following are procedural defenses against voice-cloning attacks? Select ALL that apply.
options: Use a pre-agreed shared secret (code word)
Trust the call if the voice sounds exactly right
Hang up and call back on the official directory number
Confirm high-value requests over a separate channel
practice_items.explain: Shared secrets, callback verification, and out-of-band confirmation defeat cloning. Trusting a familiar-sounding voice alone is not a reliable control as cloning quality improves.

practice_items.atom_title: Voice/image cloning for impersonation
practice_items.prompt: An attacker combines a cloned CEO voice with an urgent wire-transfer request. Which TWO cognitive shortcuts are being exploited simultaneously?
options: Reciprocity and curiosity
Scarcity and authority
Intimidation and scarcity
Recognition and urgency
practice_items.explain: The cloned voice triggers recognition ('I know this person'), while the urgent request suppresses the verification step urgency would otherwise trigger.

practice_items.atom_title: Voice/image cloning for impersonation
practice_items.prompt: Why is relying on employees to spot audio artifacts in cloned voice calls not a sustainable long-term defense strategy?
practice_items.explain: Cloning models improve continuously, so perceptual detection becomes unreliable over time. Procedural controls (shared secrets, callbacks) do not depend on cloning quality.

practice_items.atom_title: Voice/image cloning for impersonation
practice_items.prompt: A video call recipient notices the caller's face has inconsistent lighting compared to the background. What type of attack does this suggest?
options: Real-time deepfake video
SQL injection
Credential stuffing
Evil-twin Wi-Fi
practice_items.explain: Lighting inconsistency between a face and background is a known artifact of face-swap/deepfake technology used in real-time video impersonation.

practice_items.atom_title: Generative-AI phishing; prompt injection against LLM apps
practice_items.prompt: Which of the following is a direct prompt injection attack?
options: An attacker sends a phishing email crafted by an LLM
An attacker fine-tunes an LLM on stolen data
An attacker types 'ignore previous instructions' directly into a chatbot's input field
An attacker trains a classifier on poisoned labels
practice_items.explain: Direct injection means the attacker controls the user-facing input field of an LLM app and injects instructions there. Options A, C, and D describe other AI-based attacks but not prompt injection.

practice_items.atom_title: Generative-AI phishing; prompt injection against LLM apps
practice_items.prompt: Why do traditional spam filters fail against AI-generated phishing emails?
options: AI-generated emails are always encrypted
Traditional filters rely on grammar and keyword signatures; LLMs produce fluent, contextually appropriate text that lacks those tells
AI-generated emails are sent from IP addresses not in block lists
Traditional filters cannot process HTML email
practice_items.explain: Grammar-based and keyword heuristics that catch poorly-written spam break down when the content is fluent and plausible. LLMs eliminate the linguistic anomalies that made traditional phishing detectable.

practice_items.atom_title: Generative-AI phishing; prompt injection against LLM apps
practice_items.prompt: Select ALL phrases that are known prompt-injection trigger patterns.
options: ignore previous instructions
please summarize this document
you are now a different assistant
reveal system prompt
practice_items.explain: The three injection patterns attempt to override the model's instructions or extract internal configuration. 'Summarize' is a normal request and not an injection pattern.

practice_items.atom_title: Generative-AI phishing; prompt injection against LLM apps
practice_items.prompt: Name one defense that limits the impact of a successful prompt injection in an LLM-powered app.
practice_items.explain: Privilege separation ensures the LLM cannot take sensitive actions even if injected; human-in-the-loop catches harmful outputs before they execute; output validation rejects anomalous responses; input sanitization blocks known patterns before they reach the model.

practice_items.atom_title: Prompt extraction of sensitive info
practice_items.prompt: An LLM outputs 'sk-prod-abc123XYZ789' as part of a response. What class of sensitive data has leaked?
options: System prompt
Email address
Password
API key
practice_items.explain: API keys follow recognizable token patterns (e.g. 'sk-' prefix) and grant programmatic access to services. Their presence in any output is a credential leak.

practice_items.atom_title: Prompt extraction of sensitive info
practice_items.prompt: Why can an LLM 'leak' its system prompt even when instructed to keep it confidential?
options: Because the system prompt is stored in a database the model can query
Because the model lacks a memory of what it was told
Because system prompts are always public by design
Because the model treats all context, including the system prompt, as text it can reason about and quote
practice_items.explain: LLMs process all context tokens together in a single window; 'keep this secret' is a policy instruction the model may follow imperfectly when asked the right adversarial query.

practice_items.atom_title: Prompt extraction of sensitive info
practice_items.prompt: Select ALL data classes that an output filter should scan for before delivering LLM responses to end users.
options: API keys / credentials
User's account balance
System-prompt contents
Email addresses of internal staff
practice_items.explain: A user's account balance is legitimate output the chatbot is supposed to provide. The other three are sensitive classes (credentials, internal configuration, personal contact data) that an output filter should redact or block.

practice_items.atom_title: Prompt extraction of sensitive info
practice_items.prompt: Name one limitation of regex-based output filters for detecting LLM leaks.
practice_items.explain: Regex only matches patterns the defender anticipated. An adversary can evade it by rephrasing (describing the key in prose), encoding (base64), or splitting the token across sentences.

practice_items.atom_title: Prompt extraction of sensitive info
practice_items.prompt: Which architectural control best prevents a leaked API key in LLM output from being exploited?
options: Increasing the LLM's context window
Logging all LLM outputs to a SIEM
Using a larger model that is less likely to leak
Never embedding live credentials in the LLM's context in the first place
practice_items.explain: The safest control is not putting live credentials in the context at all. The LLM cannot leak what it never had. Larger models or more logging do not prevent extraction of credentials that are present.

practice_items.atom_title: False information in LLM training sets (data poisoning)
practice_items.prompt: A training sample has label='positive' and content='Worst product ever, total garbage.' What type of poisoning indicator is this?
options: Outlier marker
Distribution anomaly
Label/content mismatch
Backdoor trigger
practice_items.explain: The label directly contradicts the content's sentiment -- this is a label/content mismatch, the simplest poisoning indicator.

practice_items.atom_title: False information in LLM training sets (data poisoning)
practice_items.prompt: Which attack goal does a backdoor poisoning attack achieve?
options: Causing the model to misclassify only inputs containing a specific trigger, while behaving normally otherwise
Reducing overall model accuracy on all inputs
Increasing model training time indefinitely
Preventing the model from being fine-tuned
practice_items.explain: A backdoor is targeted: normal inputs produce normal outputs; only inputs with the trigger pattern are misclassified.

practice_items.atom_title: False information in LLM training sets (data poisoning)
practice_items.prompt: Select ALL valid indicators that a training sample may be poisoned.
options: Label directly contradicts the content
Sample length is within one standard deviation of the mean
Sample contains repeated unusual tokens or phrases
A sudden cluster of identical labels from a new data source
practice_items.explain: Normal length is not suspicious. Mismatch, unusual tokens, and sudden clusters are all poisoning indicators.

practice_items.atom_title: False information in LLM training sets (data poisoning)
practice_items.prompt: Why can a backdoor attack succeed with less than 1 percent poisoning rate?
practice_items.explain: Backdoor attacks are highly targeted: only trigger-containing inputs are affected, so the overall model appears normal and a small fraction of poisoned samples is sufficient.

practice_items.atom_title: AI reconnaissance and enhanced malware coding; defenses (shared secrets, MFA, verify output)
practice_items.prompt: A security log shows 847 DNS subdomain queries from one IP in 2 seconds. Why is this a recon indicator?
options: Normal users browse subdomains frequently during business hours
DNS queries are always malicious
The volume and speed exceed human capability, indicating automated (likely AI-assisted) subdomain enumeration
The IP address is in a known malicious range
practice_items.explain: 847 queries in 2 seconds far exceeds human browser behavior; automated tools (accelerated by AI) generate these patterns.

practice_items.atom_title: AI reconnaissance and enhanced malware coding; defenses (shared secrets, MFA, verify output)
practice_items.prompt: Which defense specifically addresses AI-generated credential stuffing attacks?
options: Increasing password length requirements
Encrypting the password database
Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
Using a web application firewall
practice_items.explain: MFA requires a second factor that AI-generated credentials cannot satisfy, blocking stuffing even when passwords are correct.

practice_items.atom_title: AI reconnaissance and enhanced malware coding; defenses (shared secrets, MFA, verify output)
practice_items.prompt: Select ALL activities that AI tools allow attackers to automate during the reconnaissance phase.
options: Scraping public profiles to build spear-phishing targets
Manually reviewing each target's email
Enumerating subdomains across thousands of targets simultaneously
Scanning CVE databases for vulnerabilities matching a target's technology stack
practice_items.explain: Manual review is not automated. Scraping, enumeration, and CVE matching are all tasks LLMs and AI tools accelerate dramatically.

practice_items.atom_title: AI reconnaissance and enhanced malware coding; defenses (shared secrets, MFA, verify output)
practice_items.prompt: Why does AI-assisted malware coding specifically threaten defenders who rely on signature-based detection?
practice_items.explain: AI can generate many syntactically varied versions of malware (polymorphic payloads); signature scanners that look for fixed byte patterns miss novel variants.

practice_items.atom_title: AI reconnaissance and enhanced malware coding; defenses (shared secrets, MFA, verify output)
practice_items.prompt: A shared secret defeats voice-cloning attacks because:
options: It encrypts the audio channel
The attacker cannot know a secret they were never trained on, and cloned audio cannot supply it dynamically
The attacker's cloned voice can reproduce any word
Shared secrets use quantum-resistant cryptography
practice_items.explain: A cloned voice can say any word it was trained on, but cannot produce a pre-agreed secret it was never exposed to, the secret is out-of-band proof of identity.
